anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between the data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and workload access patterns forces sub-optimal access paths independent of optimizer statistics.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: Physical corruption or logical inconsistency inside data pages or index structures makes stored rows or keys unreliable, causing incorrect or unstable access results.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly: Imminent or actual exhaustion of data, log, temp, or backup space prevents new allocations and halts normal database operations.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a compound failure mode in which inefficient schema design drives excessive full scans, large sorts, and frequent page splits that rapidly consume the dwindling free space, while underlying corruption causes the optimizer to discard damaged indexes or return wrong results. Symptoms include: frequent plan shifts from index seeks to full scans, exploding temp-space and log usage followed by allocation-failed errors, inconsistent row counts between index and table scans, checksum or page-level I/O errors, aborted DML/DDL due to out-of-space or corruption detection, and severe performance degradation accompanied by data-quality incidents.

Causally, poor schema and missing/inefficient indexes inflate I/O volumes and fragment structures, accelerating space consumption and triggering emergency auto-extension or allocation failures. Near-full disks, in turn, restrict the engine’s ability to split pages cleanly or rebuild indexes, increasing the likelihood of partial writes and structural corruption. Emerging block or index damage leads the optimizer to ignore or drop indexes, which amplifies the impact of the original design flaws by forcing even heavier scans that further exhaust space. Attempts to repair corruption or add corrective indexes fail due to space shortages, creating a vicious cycle where design inefficiency, structural corruption, and capacity exhaustion continuously reinforce each other and degrade both performance and data integrity across all workload types.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with logical data inconsistency, structural corruption, uniqueness conflicts, or referential-integrity rules being violated by the workload or storage state.
entry.solution_guidance: Validate data consistency, inspect constraints and index integrity, and check whether data-cleaning, repair, or workload correction is required before retrying.
